items.title: Trade Talks Collapse, Tariffs Hit at Midnight: Inside Carney's Dollar-for-Dollar Response to Trump
items.body:
## A Deadline Comes and Goes

Late Friday night, negotiators from the United States and Canada failed to reach a last-minute agreement to head off a new round of tariffs. Within hours, at the stroke of midnight, U.S. tariffs of 50% on an estimated $28 billion worth of Canadian goods took effect, marking one of the most significant escalations yet in a trade dispute that has simmered — and occasionally flared — for weeks.

The breakdown caps a period defined by starts and stops: temporary pauses, renewed threats, and rounds of talks that appeared close to a breakthrough before stalling again. According to officials familiar with the discussions, the two sides remained apart on core issues heading into the deadline, and neither delegation signaled a willingness to extend the negotiating window further.

## Carney's Response: Matching, Not Escalating

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney responded by confirming that Canada intends to impose retaliatory tariffs of equal value on U.S. goods, calibrated on a dollar-for-dollar basis, beginning September 8. Officials describe the approach as measured and proportional rather than punitive — a signal, they say, that Canada is prepared to defend its economic interests while leaving room for renewed dialogue before the retaliatory measures take effect.

The roughly two-week gap between the U.S. tariffs taking hold and Canada's countermeasures is reportedly intended to give both governments a final opportunity to return to the table. Trade analysts note that this kind of staggered response is a common negotiating tactic, designed to apply pressure without fully closing the door on a resolution.

## What's Affected

The tariffs announced by Washington reportedly touch a broad range of Canadian exports, though officials on both sides have not released a complete breakdown of the specific goods and sectors involved. Industry groups in both countries are expected to press their governments for clarity in the coming days, particularly businesses with cross-border supply chains that could face higher costs almost immediately.

Economists caution that tariffs of this scale, if sustained, tend to ripple beyond the targeted goods themselves — raising input costs for manufacturers, adding pressure on consumer prices, and creating uncertainty for companies trying to plan around cross-border trade.

## A Relationship Under Strain

The U.S. and Canada share one of the largest bilateral trading relationships in the world, and disputes of this magnitude are closely watched by businesses, investors, and policymakers on both sides of the border. This latest collapse in talks underscores how quickly negotiations can shift from cautious optimism to open confrontation, even between longtime trading partners.

Whether the two governments can find their way back to the negotiating table before September 8 remains uncertain. For now, both sides appear to be preparing for the tariffs — and the retaliation — to hold, while leaving the door open, at least rhetorically, to a future deal.

*This article reflects developments as reported and may be updated as the situation evolves.*
